article_title: Self-reported patient safety competence among Canadian medical students and postgraduate trainees: a cross-sectional survey.
citation: Doyle Patricia, VanDenKerkhof Elizabeth G, Edge Dana S, Ginsburg Liane, Goldstein David H. (2015). Self-reported patient safety competence among Canadian medical students and postgraduate trainees: a cross-sectional survey. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjqs-2014-003142
title: Reduced H-PEPSS: 16-item survey measuring six sociocultural patient safety competencies plus clinical skills, classroom and clinical settings
description: The reduced Health Professional Education in Patient Safety Survey (H-PEPSS) is a validated questionnaire measuring learners' confidence in learning six sociocultural patient safety competencies based on the Canadian Patient Safety Institute's Safety Competencies Framework, plus a clinical skills dimension of four items. Respondents answer each item separately for classroom and clinical settings on a 5-point Likert scale; the modified stem reads 'I feel confident in what I am learning about…'. Confirmatory factor analysis in both samples achieved good fit (CFI >0.95, RMSEA <0.06).
requirements: The modified present-tense stem was not validated with students, so the authors revalidated the factor structure with confirmatory factor analysis before interpreting scores
target_learning_goals: self-reported confidence in patient safety learning across six sociocultural competencies and clinical skills
examples: Administered web-based in January 2012 to 255 medical students and 141 postgraduate trainees, taking approximately 12 min to complete
key_sources: Doyle Patricia, VanDenKerkhof Elizabeth G, Edge Dana S, Ginsburg Liane, Goldstein David H. (2015). Self-reported patient safety competence among Canadian medical students and postgraduate trainees: a cross-sectional survey. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjqs-2014-003142

article_title: A student's guide to searching the literature using online databases
citation: Casey W. Miller, Michelle D. Chabot, and Troy C. Messina. (2009). A student's guide to searching the literature using online databases. Am. J. Phys., 77(12), 1112-1117. https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0931
title: Applying the h-index to a search result identifies the most influential subset of articles returned by a query
description: The article extends Hirsch's h-index from individuals to any collection of articles returned by a database search. Articles are ranked by times cited; the h-index is the rank where rank crosses citations, so "a set of articles with h = 6 has six articles each with six or more citations." Reading the top h articles samples the most influential work in an area and guides how many results to examine. The concept is illustrated in Table I and graphically in Fig. 1.
requirements: A database that reports citation counts and allows sorting results by times cited
constraints: The article states this method does not imply that articles with rank greater than h are of poor quality, since recent publications have not had time to be judged, and a highly refuted article can enter the top-cited list
target_learning_goals: locate the most highly valued articles in a field
determine how many search results to examine
examples: In the specific multiferroics deposition search, TS=multiferroic* depo* yielded 109 hits with an h of 14, and the majority of top-cited articles used pulsed laser deposition.
key_sources: Casey W. Miller, Michelle D. Chabot, and Troy C. Messina. (2009). A student's guide to searching the literature using online databases. Am. J. Phys., 77(12), 1112-1117. https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.0931
